title: Not one stone (Luke 21:1–6)
hook: the widow's mites, then the Temple's beauty and its end
tomorrow: Do this for a commemoration of me

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the middle of the palms. Your line was the things for peace. Which city did you hold? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

Two things happen in the Temple courts within six verses, and Luke sets them side by side on purpose. In the first, Jesus is watching people drop gifts into the treasury. Rich people, a steady clink of coins. Then a poor widow drops in two tiny copper coins, the smallest money there was. In the second, some people are admiring the building itself: the huge, polished stones, the gifts dedicated by the wealthy hanging on the walls. The smallest gift in the Temple, and the largest. Today, which one lasts.
screen: `THE CLINK OF RICH PEOPLE'S COINS.` → `TWO TINY COPPER COINS.` → `THE BIGGEST STONES IN THE CITY.`

segments.voice: First the widow. The Douay calls her coins two brass mites. The Greek word is lepton, which means a tiny thin thing: it was the smallest coin in use. Jesus says: "Verily I say to you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all." The others gave out of their abundance. She gave out of her want, all the living that she had. Jesus doesn't measure the amount. He measures what was left after. Then, a moment later, people are praising the Temple. And they had reason. Herod the Great had rebuilt and enlarged it on a massive scale. Josephus, who saw it, says from a distance it looked like a snowy mountain, because of the white stone and the gold. Some of its foundation stones, still visible today at the Western Wall, weigh many tons. And Jesus says: "The days will come in which there shall not be left a stone upon a stone that shall not be thrown down." Within about forty years, it happened, when Rome's army destroyed the Temple. The Western Wall that Jews pray at today is part of the retaining wall of the platform, not the Temple building itself. Put the two scenes together and they ask one question: what lasts? The great stones, admired by everyone, did not. The two coins, which nobody but Jesus noticed, are still being talked about two thousand years later, in every language the Gospel has reached. Luke isn't saying buildings are bad. Catholics build cathedrals. He's asking where your heart is resting. Stones, however beautiful, fall. A gift of the whole self is remembered.
screen: `TWO BRASS MITES: THE SMALLEST COIN.` · `MORE THAN THEY ALL.` · `A TEMPLE LIKE A SNOWY MOUNTAIN.` · `STONES FALL. THE GIFT REMAINS.` · then, large: `NOT A STONE UPON A STONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treasure what won't fall. Settle, and breathe. Make a quiet list in your head of what you're proud of, or worried about keeping: a house, a title, a body, a reputation, a bank balance. Hold each one a moment, and let it be what it is: good, and temporary. Then bring to mind something that lasts: a love you've given, a kindness someone still remembers, faith, if you have it. Rest there. If you pray, offer God something small and whole, like the widow's two coins. The bell holds the time.
Not one stone. Jesus' word about the beautiful Temple, spoken just after a poor widow's two coins: the stones will fall, the whole-hearted gift lasts. Today's word.
Your line: what lasts. Today, give one small thing with your whole heart, and let it be enough that God notices. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics bring offerings to the altar at the offertory of every Mass, and the widow's mite is often read when parishes speak of giving: not the size of the gift, but how much of yourself is in it.

fork.reveal: he says the days will come when not a stone upon a stone will remain, and about forty years later Rome destroyed it.

original.note: Greek: lepta, tiny thin coins, the smallest money in use. The Douay calls them mites.

trapdoor: what you thought: the widow's mite means small gifts are cute.
what it means: Jesus measures a gift by what's left afterward; she gave everything, and that outlasts the Temple's stones.
what a scholar hears: Josephus describes Herod's Temple as like a snow-covered mountain; it was destroyed by Rome in the year 70.

sources.quoted: Verily I say to you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all.
The days will come in which there shall not be left a stone upon a stone that shall not be thrown down.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 21:3 and 21:6, and 'two brass mites' in 21:2.
Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.6 (5.222–223): the Temple appeared to strangers like a mountain covered with snow. Paraphrased; confirm.
Western Wall as part of the retaining wall of the Temple Mount: standard; confirm phrasing is respectful to Jewish readers.
Yesterday's script quoted the stone-upon-stone theme (19:44) only in paraphrase; today quotes 21:6. Confirm the two days don't overlap too much.
